background_knowledge: Kurt_Edward_Fishback

Kurt Edward Fishback is an American photographer noted for his portraits of other artists and photographers. He is the son of photographer Glen Fishback and namesake of photographer Edward Weston. Kurt studied art at Sacramento City College, SFAI, Cornell University and UC Davis where he received his Master of Fine Arts Degree studying with Robert Arneson, Roy DeForest, William Wiley and Manuel Neri. The series of artist portraits which now number over 250 were begun in 1979. Other artist portraits made by Kurt include Cornell Capa, André Kertész, Mary Ellen Mark, Chuck Close and Robert Mapplethorpe.

background_knowledge: Jacques_Brugnon

Jacques 'Toto' Brugnon was a French tennis player. He won 10 Grand Slam doubles titles in the French, American, Australian and British championships. He was part of the famous Four Musketeers team that conquered the Cup in 1927 against the USA. He played in 20 Wimbledon Championships between 1920 and 1948 and achieved his best singles result in 1926 when he reached the semifinals, losing in a close five set match to Howard Kinsey. Between 1921 and 1934 he played 31 ties for the French Davis Cup team, mainly as a doubles player, and compiled a record of 26 wins versus 11 losses. He never won a Major title but won two mixed doubles titles at Roland Garros.

background_knowledge: Georgy_Grechko

Georgy Mikhaylovich Grechko (born May 25, 1931) is a retired Soviet cosmonaut. He flew on several space flights including Soyuz 17, Soyuz 26, and Soyuz T-14. He made the first spacewalk in an Orlan space suit on December 20, 1977 during the Salyut 6 EO-1 mission. He was twice awarded the medal of Hero of the Soviet Union. He resigned from the space programme in 1992 to lecture on atmospheric physics at the Russian Academy of Sciences. He established the Association of Space Explorers in 1984, which is open to all people who have flown in outer space. A minor planet discovered by Soviet astronomer Nikolai Stepanovich Chernykh is named after him.

background_knowledge: Rolf_Disch

Rolf Disch is a German architect, solar energy pioneer and environmental activist. He has led Germany as the solar pioneer in respect to residential, retail and commercial building and design. In 1994, he built the Heliotrope in Freiburg which was the world’s first home to create more energy than it uses. In June 2009, Disch launched the 100% GmbH organization, with the aim to make Freiburger and its surrounding district the first 100% sustainable renewable energy region in the world. He currently owns his own architecture firm, Rolfdisch Solar Architecture. He is also the owner of PlusEnergy, a company that sells surplus solar energy back into the grid for profit.

background_knowledge: Lawrence_S._Trimble

Lawrence Strother Trimble was born in Fleming County, Kentucky in 1825. He was a slave-holder up to the Civil War. Trimble served three consecutive terms in the U.S. House of Representatives from 1865 to 1870 as a Democrat for the 1st Congressional District of Kentucky. In 1879, Trimble moved to Albuquerque, New Mexico, where he continued the practice of law and again entered politics. He gave the opening address at the New Mexico Constitutional Convention of 1889. He died in Albuquerque, August 9, 1904, and was buried in the Fairview Cemetery off of Yale Boulevard. It is unclear whether he was a Republican or a Democrat.

background_knowledge: Adrian_Aeschbacher

Adrian Aeschbacher (10 May 1912 in Langenthal, Switzerland – 9 November 2002 in Zurich) was a Swiss classical pianist. He became famous as an interpreter of Ludwig van Beethoven, Franz Schubert, Robert Schumann and Johannes Brahms. He recorded for Decca among other labels. From 1965 until 1977 he taught at the Hochschule des Saarlandes fur Musik in Saarbrücken. His notable students included Peter Schmalfuss. His father was professor of piano at the Conservatoire of Trogen in Zürich, where he spent his youth.

background_knowledge: Ernest_Nash

Ernest Nash was a student of Roman architecture and pioneer of archaeological photography. Nash first went to Italy on August 30, 1936 with a goal of documenting in photographs the ancient ruins of Rome, Ostia, and Pompeii. He emigrated to the United States in 1939, but returned to Italy in 1952 to continue his work. He established the Fototeca Unione archive at the American Academy in Rome in 1957 and served as its director. Besides architectural photography he also produced a series of portraits of famous musicians, including Béla Bartók, while he lived in New York City. He is survived by his third wife, two daughters, two grandchildren and now two great grand children.

background_knowledge: Alan_Lee_(footballer)

Alan Desmond Lee (born 21 August 1978) is a Irish former footballer who played as a striker. He is now working as an academy coach at Ipswich Town. He scored 119 goals in 547 appearances in a 19-year professional career in the Football League, and won 10 caps for the Republic of Ireland. He started his career with Aston Villa, also playing on loan at Torquay United and Port Vale. After a season with Burnley, he signed with Rotherham United in 2000. He was then bought by Cardiff City, and made almost 100 appearances for the Welsh side between 2003 and 2006. He then moved to Ipswich before earning a big money move to Crystal Palace. He wrote himself into the club's folklore by scoring in the final game of the 2009–10 season against Sheffield Wednesday, saving the Eagles from relegation and ultimately administration.

background_knowledge: Daniella_Smith

Daniella Smith is a New Zealand former professional boxer. She is the first International Boxing Federation Women's World Champion. Smith is also ranked pound-for-pound number one in New Zealand of all time in the Women's division. These days Smith co-owns a boxing gym called Boxing Alley. She also trains corporate and amateur boxers. Smith also competed in 2002 World Championships in Turkey, even though she was not successful on winning a medal, she still won a gold medal in 2004 at the Oceania Games. In 2014, Smith fought her last fight against Gentiane Lupi, but this time for the vacant NZPBA women's lightweight title.

background_knowledge: Ross_Hutchins

Ross Dan Hutchins is a retired British professional tennis player. He is known best as a doubles player, who achieved a highest doubles ranking of 26. On 24 December 1807 he witnessed the wreck of the Anson frigate in Mount's Bay, when over a hundred lives were lost, and this disaster led him to devote his life and patrimony to the discovery of some means for saving lives at shipwrecks. He spent much labour in attempting to devise a lifeboat, but produced no satisfactory results, and turned his attention to the 'Rocket' life- saving apparatus, an early form of the Breeches buoy. He was dismayed at the then common practice of burying victims of shipw wreck in common graves in unconsecrated ground near the site of the wreck.

background_knowledge: James_Lonsdale-Bryans

James Lonsdale-Bryans (1893-1981) was a British writer, amateur diplomat and Nazi sympathiser. He travelled to Italy to meet Ulrich von Hassell, the German ambassador to Italy in 1940. He believed Von Hassell would be receptive to the idea of a pact between Britain and Germany at the outbreak of World War II. The terms of this pact were that Germany would have a free hand in Europe in return for Britain running the rest of the world. However, he unsuccessfully attempted to arrange a meeting with both U.S. General Dwight D. Eisenhower and British General Bernard Montgomery. MI5 decided against having him arrested, due to the possible support he was receiving from members of Parliament (potentially including Neville Chamberlain), and the embarrassment this would have caused.

background_knowledge: Ben_Weese

Benjamin Horace (Ben) Weese (born 1929) is an American architect. He is a member of the architects group, the Chicago Seven. Weese is the younger brother of fellow Chicago architect Harry Weese. He received his B.Arch. and his M. Arch. from Harvard University and a certificate from the École des Beaux-Arts in Fontainebleau, France. He returned to Chicago in 1957 into his older brother's firm. In 1977, he opened his own firm, Weese Seegers Hickey Weese, with his wife. This turned out to be an award-winning firm and was best known for non-profit and educational projects with an emphasis on historical appreciation and preservation.

background_knowledge: Barbara_Barrett

Barbara Barrett was U.S. Ambassador to Finland from 2008 to 2009. Barrett was the first female Republican candidate for Governor of Arizona in 1994. Barrett earned her bachelor's, master's and law degrees at Arizona State University. She was a partner in a large Phoenix law firm and, before she was thirty, she was an executive of two global Fortune 500 companies. She and her husband Craig own Triple Creek Ranch in Montana, named by Travel + Leisure as the best hotel in the world for 2014. Barrett is chairman of the Aerospace Corporation and a member of the boards of California Institute of Technology, Sally Ride Science, RAND Corporation, Smithsonian Institution and Horatio Alger Association of Distinguished Americans. Barrett is the first civilian woman to land in an F/A-18 Hornet on an aircraft carrier. She has trained as an astronaut, and was the backup spaceflight participant for the Soyuz TMA-16 flight to the International Space Station. She climbed Tanzania's Mt. Kilimanjaro in August 2007 and bicycled 900 kilometers around Finland while Ambassador. In 2014, Barrett received the Worcester Polytechnic Institute Presidential Medal from President Laurie Leshin. She also received the Defense Medal for Exceptional Public Service, Horatio Alger Award for Distinguished Americans, Woodrow Wilson Award for Corporate Citizenship and Sandra Day O’Connor Board Excellence Award.

background_knowledge: Frank_Gardner_(racing_driver)

Frank Gardner OAM (1 October 1931 – 29 August 2009) was a racing driver from Australia. He was European F5000 champion, and participated in nine World Championship Formula One Grands Prix, debuting on 11 July 1964. Gardner also participated in numerous non-Championship Formula One races and his results included a third placing at the 1965 Mediterranean Grand Prix at the Autodromo di Pergusa in Sicily. He participated each year in the open wheeler Tasman Series held in New Zealand and Australia during the European winter, and shared the grids with the likes of Jim Clark, Graham Hill and Jochen Rindt.

background_knowledge: Max_Yalden

Maxwell Freeman Yalden, CC (April 12, 1930 – February 9, 2015) was a Canadian civil servant and diplomat. He was Ambassador to Belgium and Luxembourg from 1984 to 1987. From 1987 to 1996 he was the Chief Commissioner of the Canadian Human Rights Commission. He died at Ottawa, Ontario, at age 84, from pneumonia complications. He received a Bachelor of Arts degree from the University of Toronto in 1952 and a Ph.D in 1956 from Michigan. In 1988 he was made an Officer of the Order of Canada and was promoted to Companion in 1999. In 1998 he was awarded an Honorary LL.D. from Carleton University.

background_knowledge: Ankō_Asato

Anko Asato (1827 – 1906) was a Ryūkyūan master of karate. He and Ankō Itosu were the two main karate masters who taught Gichin Funakoshi. Asato's family belonged to the Tunchi class, and held authority in the village of Asato, halfway between Shuri and Naha. He was also skilled at riding horses, Jigen-ryū kendō (swordsmanship), archery, and an exceptional scholar. He set a trap for troublemakers in his home village, and defeated a man armed with an unblunted blade.

background_knowledge: Mary_Lou_Foy

Mary Lou Foy is an American photojournalist. She served as Picture Editor at the Washington Post from 1990 to 2006. Foy was president of the National Press Photographers Association in 1992. She received the Samuel Mellor Award in 1984, the Joseph Costa Award in 1998, the Morris Berman NPPA Citation in 2003, and twice received the NPPA's President's Award in1984 and 1986. She is a graduate of the University of Florida in journalism and environmental engineering. She was also the first female photojournalists to work for the Gainesville Sun and the Miami Herald, as well as the Fort Lauderdale Sun-Sentinel.

Lucien Buysse (11 September 1892 – 3 January 1980) was a Belgian cyclist and a champion of the Tour de France. He won the 1926 Tour after taking the yellow jersey from Gustave Van Slembrouck on stage 10. He entered the Tour in 1914 but did not finish. In 1923 he completed the Tour and finished in eighth place. In the 1924 and 1925 Tours, he rode with the Italian Automoto team led by Ottavio Bottecchia, where he was perhaps the first domestique in the Tour. He placed third in 1924 and second in 1925. The 1926 Tour was the longest in its history (5,745 km), with 17 stages averaging 338 km.

John Hunter FRS (13 February 1728 – 16 October 1793) was a Scottish surgeon, one of the most distinguished scientists and surgeons of his day. He was a teacher of, friend of, and collaborator with, Edward Jenner, the inventor of the smallpox vaccine. His wife, Anne Hunter (née Home), was a minor poet, some of whose poems were set to music by Joseph Haydn. He learned anatomy by assisting his elder brother William with dissections in William's anatomy school in London, starting in 1748, and quickly became expert in anatomy. He built up a collection of living animals whose skeletons and other organs he prepared as anatomical specimens, eventually amassing nearly 14,000 preparations demonstrating the anatomy of humans.

Homer Baxter Sprague (October 19, 1829 - March 23, 1918) was an American author, educator, abolitionist, and Lieutenant Colonel of the Union Army. Sprague was a Captain of the 13th Connecticut Infantry Regiment in 1861 when the American Civil War began. He quickly rose to the rank of Colonel before being captured as a prisoner of war by the Confederate Army in 1864. In 1865 he was released in a prisoner exchange, and remained active within the military until the end of the war. An early progressive voice in education, he served as president of Adelphi Academy in New York as it first opened its doors to female students. While there, he institutionalized the first fire drills in the United States school system.

background_knowledge: Richard_Crawford_White

Richard Crawford White (April 29, 1923 – February 18, 1998) was a Democratic politician from El Paso, Texas. He served in the Texas House of Representatives from 1955 to 1959 and in the U.S. House of Reps. from 1965 to 1983. White served in World War II as a rifleman and Japanese-English interpreter in the Pacific Theater. He was awarded the Purple Heart for his actions in the war. He also served as the El Paso County Democratic chairman from 1963 to 1965. White was elected to the historic Eighty-ninth Congress as part of the national 1964 Democratic surge linked to President Lyndon B. Johnson's crushing defeat of Republican Senator Barry M. Goldwater. White served in the U.S. Senate from Texas from 1971 to 1982. He served on the Interior, Post Office & Civil Service, and Science & Technology committees. White was married twice. His ashes are interred at Arlington National Cemetery, in Arlington, Virginia, near the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier, in area 7A. White died on February 18, 1998, in El Paso, Texas. His first marriage in 1949 to Katherine Huffman produced three sons, Rodrick, Richard, and Raymond. After her death in 1972, White married the former Kathleen Fitzgerald in 1973. The second marriage produced one daughter, Bonnie, two sons, Sean and Brian, and one step-son, Kenneth.

Hancock, the infamous Black Sox Scandal gambler, Arnold Rothstein, Morton L. Schwartz, Jane Greer, and Virginia Fair Vanderbilt. Max Hirsch won the first of his four Belmont Stakes in 1928 with Vito. In 1936, he won the Kentucky Derby and Preakness Stakes with Bold Venture and in 1946 captured the U.S. Triple Crown with Assault. His son, Buddy, followed in his footsteps and too was voted into the U.-S. RacingHall of Fame.

background_knowledge: Jim_Umbricht

James Umbricht was an American professional baseball player. He played between 1959 and 1963 for the Pittsburgh Pirates and Houston Colt .45s. Diagnosed with malignant melanoma in March 1963, his comeback to baseball following surgery made national headlines and encouraged research on the disease. He died within six months, from complications from melanoma, in a Houston area hospital at age 33. His ashes were spread over the construction site of the Astrodome, the future home of the Colt . 45s. The team retired his jersey number, 32, and wore black armbands for the 1964 season in his honor. They also retired his number, 29, for the 1965 season.

background_knowledge: Luis_Herrera_(cyclist)

Luis Alberto Herrera (born May 4, 1961 in Fusagasugá, Colombia), is a retired Colombian road racing cyclist. Herrera was a professional from 1985 to 1992 but had a successful amateur career before that in Colombia. His greatest achievement was in 1987, when he won the Vuelta a España, the first South American to win a Grand Tour. Herrera also won the Critérium du Dauphiné Libéré in 1988 and 1991 and five \"King of the Mountains\" jerseys from the three Grand Tours. Luis Herrera is the second rider to win the King of the Mountain jersey in all three Grand Tours.

background_knowledge: Tom_Perriello

Thomas Stuart Price \"Tom\" Perriello is an American attorney, diplomat and Democratic Party politician. He served one term as a U.S. Representative for Virginia's 5th congressional district, serving from 2009 until 2011. He was the United States Special Representative for the Quadrennial Diplomacy and Development Review from 2014 to 2015. He has also been the Special Envoy for the African Great Lakes and the Congo-Kinshasa since 2015. A populist Democrat, he was a key ally in Congress of President Barack Obama and was narrowly defeated in the 2010 election by Republican State Senator Robert Hurt. After leaving office, he served as President and CEO of the Center for American Progress Action Fund and as a Counselor for Policy at Center forAmerican Progress.

background_knowledge: Catherine_Small_Long

Catherine Small Long is a Democratic former U.S. representative from Louisiana. She served from 1985 to 1987, the remainder of the term of her husband, Gillis William Long, after his death. Long represented the since disbanded Eighth Congressional District based in central Louisiana about Alexandria. She was the first female veteran elected to Congress, having served as a WAVE in the United States Navy. With her husband Gillis, Long had two children, George Harrison Long (born October 13, 1954) and Janis Catherine Long ( born March 25, 1957). Cathy Long resides in Chevy Chase, Maryland. In his autobiography, former lieutenant governor and education superintendent William J. Dodd, an astute observer of Louisiana politics for a half century, describes Cathy Long, who compiled a liberal voting record in Congress, as the "perfect political wife"

background_knowledge: Kelly_Johnson_(engineer)

Clarence Leonard \"Kelly\" Johnson (February 27, 1910 – December 21, 1990) was an American aeronautical and systems engineer. He is recognized for his contributions to a series of important aircraft designs, most notably the Lockheed U-2 and SR-71 Blackbird. As a member and first team leader of the Lockheed Skunk Works, Johnson worked for more than four decades. He played a leading role in the design of over forty aircraft, including several honored with the prestigious Collier Trophy. Johnson was ranked 8th on Aviation Week & Space Technology's list of the top 100 \"most important, most interesting, and most influential people\" in the first century of aerospace.

background_knowledge: Jehane_Benoît

Jehane Benoît was a Canadian culinary author, speaker, commentator, journalist, and broadcaster. She studied at the Sorbonne and the Cordon Bleu cooking school in Paris. She wrote 30 books during her career, including the Encyclopedia of Canadian Cuisine. In 1973, she was made an Officer of the Order of Canada for her contribution to this art in Canada. She appeared regularly on CBC Television's Take 30. She later became a proponent of microwave cookery, writing several books on the subject as well as appearing in television commercials for Panasonic microwaves. In 2012, Marguerite Paulin and Marie Desjardins published a biography of Jehane BenOît, le roman de la grande dame de la cuisine canadienne.

background_knowledge: Chu_Shong-tin

He is known as the 'King of Siu Nim Tao', Wing Chun's most important form and its crucial foundation. background_knowledge: Ludwig_Obry

Ludwig Obry was an Austrian engineer and naval officer of the Austrian Navy. He invented a gyroscopic device for steering a torpedo in 1895. The device consisted of a bronze wheel weighing less than 1.5 pounds that was spun by an air jet. Obry then patented his device and sold the rights to Robert Whitehead, who incorporated the mechanism into the Whitehead torpedo. The gyroscope was invented by Leon Foucault in 1851 but industry ignored the device for nearly 50 years. In 1895 or 1896, Obry rediscovered FouCault's device and adapted it into a mechanism for steering the torpedo. This increased the weapon's accuracy from hundreds to thousands of yards.

background_knowledge: Abe_Segal

Alan Abraham Segal (23 October 1930 – 4 April 2016) was a South African tennis player. During the 1950s and 1960s, he was the doubles partner of Gordon Forbes. In 1951 he won the singles title at the Irish Open defeating Guy Jackson in the final in straight sets. He played for the South African Davis Cup team in 19 ties in the years 1955, 57, 59, 61-65 and compiled a record of 24 wins and 14 losses. After retiring from tennis, Segal took up painting. In 2008 he published a memoir titled Hey Big Boy!. Segal died of cancer on 4 April 2014 at the age of 85.

background_knowledge: John_Plumb

John Plumb (6 February 1927 – 6 April 2008) was an English abstract painter who emerged in Britain after World War II. Plumb's works reflected his admiration for American Color Field painting and hard-edge painting. In the mid-1960s Plumb produced paintings with large fields of a single color; with narrow, strips on the edge of different colors intended to enhance the emotional impact of the central, major, and usually intense hue. He taught at Bennington College in Vermont in 1968 and 1969. When he died, Plumb was 81 years old. He was married to Joan Lawrence, a long-time close friend.

background_knowledge: Mary_Gow

Mary Lightbody Gow (London 25 December 1851 – 27 May 1929 London) was an English watercolour painter. She painted mostly figures and genre in watercolours, especially young girls. She was a member of the Royal Institute of Painters in Watercolour from 1875 until her resignation in 1903. Her painting, Marie-Antoinette, was purchased under the Chantrey bequest in 1908. Her husband was the genre painter Sydney Prior Hall (1842–1922) whom she married in 1907. Her work Mother and Child was included in the book Women Painters of the World. She also exhibited at the Royal Academy from 1873 and the New Gallery and the Royal Birmingham Society of Artists.

She started out as a mannequin for Paul Poiret, which she credited with helping her learn to 'understand the female body' She was head of the workroom at Vionnet until she left to launch her own couture house in December 1928. Her heirs presented a 1948 evening gown that she had designed to the Musée Galliera.

background_knowledge: Carlos_Pérez_(radiation_oncologist)

background_knowledge: Charles_Inglis_(engineer)

Sir Charles Edward Inglis, OBE, FRS (31 July 1875 – 19 April 1952) was a British civil engineer. He served in the Royal Engineers during the First World War. In 1916 he was placed in charge of bridge design and supply at the War Office. With Giffard Le Quesne Martel, he pioneered the use of temporary bridges with tanks. He returned to Cambridge University after the war as a professor and head of the Engineering Department. Under his leadership, the department became the largest in the university and one of the best regarded engineering schools in the world. He has been described as the greatest teacher of engineering of his time.

background_knowledge: Pauline_Bewick

In 2006 she donated a collection of 200 works including tapestries, wall hangings, watercolours and sketches to the state. They are now on permanent display in the Walton Building at the Waterford Institute of Technology, and in the Killorglin Library, Co. Kerry. background_knowledge: Johnny_Leach

John Alfred Leach MBE was a British table tennis player, coach, and author. In 1949, he became Great Britain's second World Champion singles player. Two years later, he added a second singles title. In 1953, he was part of the team that won Britain's first, and as of 2014 only, team World Championship. He also won 13 bronze and silver World championship medals between 1947 and 1955. As of 2014, Leach is just one of 11 players from any country to win two singles championships. He was England's national coach for eight years and served as president of the English Table Tennis Association for more than 20 years. He continued to write a column for News of the World for twenty years.

background_knowledge: Gregory_Mangin

During WWII Mangin enlisted in the United States Army Air Forces (AAF) and flew 50 missions over Europe. Reaching the rank of staff sergeant he received the Distinguished Flying Cross (DFC), the Air Medal with six clusters and a Purple Heart with one cluster. Mangin died in October 1979 at the age of 66. He leaves behind a wife, Carol and a son, Robert.

He designed and built his own panoramic cameras which he used to take all of his photographs. Two of Avison's handmade cameras as well as models and notes were donated to the George Eastman House on his death in 2004. He worked as an instructor of physics at Brown University from 1959 to 1966 and at Purdue University from 1967 to 1969. He received his Ph.D. in Physics from Brown University in 1966 and an M.S. in photography from the Illinois Institute of Chicago's Institute of Design.

background_knowledge: John_Holmes_Jellett

John Holmes Jellett OBE, DSc, MA (1905–1971) was a British civil engineer. He served in the Royal Navy Volunteer Reserve during the Second World War and was commissioned as a Temporary Captain. His engineering talents were called upon during the Invasion of Normandy where he was made Superintending Civil Engineer of Mulberry Harbour B, a temporary concrete harbour built at Arromanches. Mulberry B was in use for five months following the invasion and landed two million men, half a million vehicles and four million tons of supplies for the Liberation of Europe. He was appointed an Officer of the Order of the British Empire (military division) on 28 November 1944.

background_knowledge: Johann_Karl_Wilhelm_Illiger

Johann Karl Wilhelm Illiger (19 November 1775 – 10 May 1813) was a German entomologist and zoologist. Illiger was professor and director of the zoological museum in Berlin from its formation in 1810 until his death. In 1811 he introduced the taxonomic order Proboscidea for elephants, the American mastodon and the wooly mammoth. He also described the subspecies Odobenus rosmarus divergens, commonly known as the Pacific walrus. His macaw and saddle-back tamarin commemorate his name. The botanical genus Illigera (family Hernandiaceae) also bears his name and is named after him.

background_knowledge: Marvin_Camras

Marvin Camras was an electrical engineer and inventor who was widely influential in the field of magnetic recording. Camras built his first recording device, a wire recorder, in the 1930s for a cousin who was an aspiring singer. He discovered that using magnetic tape made the process of splicing and storing recordings easier. In June 1944 he was awarded U.S. Patent 2,351,004, titled \"Method and Means of Magnetic Recording\". In all, Camras received more than 500 patents, largely in theField of electronic communications. He died of kidney failure at the age of 79 in Evanston, Illinois. In recognition of his achievements, he received the National Medal of Technology in 1990.

From 1875 to 1878 he was educated in the Technical Department of the cantonal school in Aarau. After a commercial apprenticeship in Geneva, he managed the straw goods factory. He collected insects in his spare time, encouraged by the curator of the Entomological collections of the University of Geneva Dr. Emil Frey-Gessner (1826–1917). In addition to his own collections, he purchased world Coleoptera and plant collections.

background_knowledge: Wang_Maozhai

The beginnings of Wu-style were created by a Manchurian named Wu Quanyou (1834–1902) Wu was a student of Yang Luchan, (founder of the Yang style), and Yang Banhou. His son, Wu Jianquan (1870–1942), loved martial arts from his youth and studied under the tutorship of his father. After 1912 he continuously developed the teaching t'ai chi ch'uan at the Beijing Sport Research Society, gradually refining his father’s style to what is currently recognised as Wu- style. His primary disciple was Yang Yuting. Wang Maozhai (1862–1940) was one of his three primary disciples. In 1929, the first documentary book on Wu- Style Tai Chi Chuan was published by Wu Chien-ch'uan, Wang Maozai and Guo Fen.

background_knowledge: Reg_Parnell

Reginald Harold Haslam Parnell (2 July 1911 – 7 January 1964) was a racing driver and team manager from Derby, England. He participated in seven Formula One World Championship Grands Prix, achieving one podium, and scoring a total of nine championship points. He was banned following an accident with Kay Petre which ended her racing career. He later raced a whole host of cars before turning to management and taking Aston Martin into Formula 1. He had a considerable influence on post-war British motorsport until his premature death in 1964. He bought up racing cars before the war. Once the hostilities had ceased he sold them to form the basis of post- war racing entries. His son Tim later raced in Formula 1 himself.

background_knowledge: William_Barton_Wade_Dent

William Barton Wade Dent (September 8, 1806 – September 7, 1855) was an American politician, educator, soldier and businessman from Georgia. He represented Georgia in the U.S. Congress (1853–1855) Dent was born in Bryantown, Maryland, in 1806 and attended Charlotte Hall Military Academy in Charlotte Hall, Maryland. In 1827, Dent pursued mercantile interests in Bullsboro, Georgia, and was also a key founding member of the city of Newnan, Georgia. Dent also served as a colonel in the Georgia Militia during the Creek War. He returned to Newnan in 1849 and presided as judge of the inferior court of Coweta County.

background_knowledge: Ferhunde_Erkin

Ferhunde Erkin was a Turkish pianist born in Istanbul in 1909. She made the first playings of 22 piano concertos in Turkey. She played in Berlin at wartime in 1943 with Berlin City Orchestra conducted by Fritz Zaun. She retired in 1967 and died in Istanbul on July 11, 2007. She received the Sevda-Cenap And Music Foundation Honour medal in 1999. Some of her students are Hüseyin Sermet, Nimet Karatekin, composer Nevit Kodallı, Kamuran Gündemir, Filiz Ali, Madlen Saydam, Tekin Alp Ulusoy and Zeren Dirim.

background_knowledge: Charles_Peake

Sir Charles Brinsley Pemberton Peake GCMG MC (2 January 1897 – 10 April 1958) was a British diplomat. Peake served in the Royal Leicestershire Regiment during the First World War, being commissioned into the 1/4th Battalion in 1915. He was awarded the Military Cross in June 1916. He joined Her Majesty's Diplomatic Service in 1922. His first appointment was in Sofia, subsequently being posted to Tokyo, Paris, Washington DC and Tangier. In 1946 he became Ambassador to Yugoslavia, before his appointment as Ambassador to Greece in 1951. In 1956 he was invested as a Knight Grand Cross of the Order of St Michael and St George.

background_knowledge: Dick_Hern

William Richard \"Dick\" Hern, CVO, (20 January 1921 – 22 May 2002) was an English Thoroughbred racehorse trainer and winner of sixteen British Classic Races between 1962 and 1995. Hern became a St. Leger Stakes specialist, winning the event six times. He produced three Epsom Derby winners in Troy (1979), Henbit (1980) and Nashwan (1989), who also won the 2,000 Guineas and the King George VI and Queen Elizabeth Stakes. In 1988 he was controversially sacked from his position as trainer for Queen Elizabeth II at West Ilsley by her racing manager 7th Earl of Carnarvon – Hern was recovering from heart surgery at the time.

His father was the well known modern architect Guillermo Bermú dez Umaña and her mother Graciela Samper Gnecco. He graduated in Architecture in 1973. Since 1975 he has been a faculty member of the Universidad de Los Andes teaching at the Department of Architecture. His work is less propositive and less innovative, but his involvement with pedagogy has provided him a position of certain relevance in Bogota's architectural context.

background_knowledge: Lee_Weiss

Lee Weiss is an American painter. She won numerous watercolor awards, as well as exhibiting in the White House Rotating Exhibition Program. She painted her impressions of a space shuttle launch in 1984, under the auspices of the NASA art program. Weiss invented a watercolor technique in which she paints both sides of the paper, turning the paper back and forth while the paint is still wet. She works away from the subject matter, in the studio without sketches or slides, allowing the process of painting to guide the portrayal. Her work is part of over sixty corporate and museum collections. She has held solo exhibitions in California, Iowa, Michigan, Minnesota, and Wisconsin, and taking part in group exhibitions in Japan and France.
